examples.question: Should Koppert develop a differentiated proposition for home gardeners, building on its biological crop protection for professional growers, or stay with professional growers? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Home gardeners will adopt Koppert's biological controls if they perceive them as convenient, easy to use, and safe for children and pets, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay a premium.
theories.T2: Home gardeners will adopt Koppert's biological controls if they perceive them as a status symbol or a way to differentiate their garden, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay a premium.

arguments.recommendation: Take a test-first move into home gardeners rather than a full launch or staying professional-only. Koppert already reaches this segment and regulation (France banning amateur pesticide sales from January 2019) favours biologicals, but no source shows demand or willingness to pay. Keep the professional core; run a bounded real-purchase pilot and commit only if actual orders clear a pre-set threshold.
arguments.target_customer: Existing home-gardener buyers of Koppert beneficial insects — amateur gardeners, especially in markets such as France where chemical options for amateurs are being phased out.
arguments.value_proposition: Convenient, safe, easy-to-use biological pest control for the home garden, backed by Koppert's professional-grower reputation and existing reach to home-gardening enthusiasts.
arguments.next_action: Run a bounded pilot: list one beneficial-insect product via existing home-gardener retail/DTC reach (koppert-lo-canada), track paid orders and repeat use over 12 weeks, with a pre-set go/no-go threshold.
arguments.uncertainty: Whether home gardeners buy biological controls in volume at a price covering retail costs; no source shows demand, WTP, or repeat use.
would_change_if: A real-purchase pilot shows conversion below a pre-set threshold or willingness to pay below cost.
Regulation keeps amateur chemical pesticides widely available in Koppert's target markets, removing the substitution driver.

justification.learned: Sources show Koppert already reaches home gardeners: koppert-lo-canada serves 'both the professional grower and the home gardening enthusiast'; koppert-martha-visit shows an on-site home-garden plan; koppert-wsu-shipped notes lady beetles are 'shipped to farmers and home gardeners alike'. These establish supply capability and reach, not demand. koppert-agro-ban reports France banning amateur pesticide sales from January 2019, a regulatory push toward biologicals. T1 (convenience/safety) is favoured over T2 (status) mainly because safety aligns with that substitution driver; neither has demand, WTP or adoption evidence.
justification.uncertain: Demand is unknown: no source measures home-gardener purchase intent, WTP, adoption or repeat use. koppert-lo-canada and koppert-wsu-shipped are neutral on motivation; koppert-martha-visit is one celebrity anecdote. It is unclear whether T1 or T2 drives buying, or whether home gardeners buy biologicals at all at a price covering Koppert's retail costs. The regulatory tailwind (koppert-agro-ban) may create necessity-driven substitution, but no source quantifies it.
justification.why_next: The proposed test X1 varies only package wording and measures stated purchase intent, so it cannot separate T1 from T2 or show real demand; I would not run it as specified. The next step should observe consequential behaviour: a bounded pilot listing a real simplified Koppert beneficial-insect product through existing home-gardener channels and measuring actual paid orders and repeat purchase. This acts on koppert-lo-canada (existing retail reach) and koppert-agro-ban (regulatory opening), and gives T1 and T2 a discriminating behavioural signal.

Use retail packaging and direct-to-consumer channels to reach home gardeners, while monitoring actual purchase behavior throu…
arguments.target_customer: Home gardeners who grow vegetables, fruits, or flowers and are willing to adopt biological controls as an alternative to chemical pesticides.
arguments.value_proposition: A convenient, safe, and easy-to-use retail package of biological controls (e.g., lady beetles) that delivers effective pest control without chemical residues, positioned as a trusted professional‑grade solution for the home gardener.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Home Gardener Proposition Test (500 respondents, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for convenience‑focused versus status‑focused packages.
arguments.uncertainty: Actual purchase behavior and willingness to pay for a convenience‑focused proposition; the extent to which home gardeners value status signaling; and the feasibility of reaching home gardeners through retail channels.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the convenience package is at least 20 percentage points higher than for the status package, or if willingness to pay for convenience exceeds status by a significant margin, we would shift toward a T1‑

If the test shows no meaningful difference or status package outperforms convenience, we would reconsider the strategy and possibly explore a status‑focused proposition or stay with professional growers.
If new evidence shows strong home‑gardener demand for biological controls driven by status signaling, we would revise the recommendation to prioritize a status‑focused proposition.

examples.question: It is mid-2014. Should ResMed develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its non-contact sleep-sensing technology and sleep-medicine expertise? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Individuals with sleep apnoea will adopt a home sleep test device if they perceive it as convenient and accurate, and if they are willing to pay a premium for non-contact technology that avoids the need for clinic visits.
theories.T2: Insurance companies will cover home sleep tests if they are validated against polysomnography and demonstrate clinical efficacy, leading consumers to adopt home testing because they avoid clinic visits and reduce out-of-pocket costs.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a full consumer launch yet. ResMed has a real non-contact sleep-sensing capability and sleep-medicine expertise, but no source demonstrates that individual sleep-apnoea patients will pay for it. Make the investment conditional: run the willingness-to-pay test first, and invest in a differentiated consumer home-testing proposition only if diagnosed patients show premium willingness to pay.
arguments.target_customer: Individuals with diagnosed or suspected sleep apnoea who today reach ResMed through sleep clinics and home healthcare dealers (resmed-10k-clinics) - the group for whom a touch-free home sensor removes a clinic visit and wiring.
arguments.value_proposition: A convenient, touch-free home sensor that measures sleep and breathing, built on ResMed's sleep-medicine expertise and non-contact sensing validated against polysomnography (resmed-pr-biancamed; brief).
arguments.next_action: Run X1 (EUR 15,000, 10 weeks, 300 adults): invest only if diagnosed patients show WTP >=$150 and >=30% intent; if <=$100 and <=20%, hold and test B2B/insurer demand. Prefer deposits to stated intent.
arguments.uncertainty: No source shows actual consumer demand or willingness to pay. The 2011 study's 78% accuracy and kappa 0.38, lower in the high-AHI group, weakens the accuracy mechanism for the targeted patients. Insurer coverage (T2) is unproven.
would_change_if: If X1 shows WTP at or below $100 and intent at most 20% among diagnosed patients (T2 outcome), abandon the consumer route and test insurer/B2B demand instead.
If independent evidence emerges that individuals already buy home sleep tests at a premium, invest without waiting for X1.

justification.learned: resmed-10k-clinics shows ResMed markets primarily to home healthcare dealers and sleep clinics; resmed-10k-dealer shows products are bought by dealers who sell to the patient, so individuals are reached only indirectly. resmed-pr-biancamed confirms a non-contact SleepMinder exists for home/hospital use. resmed-pm-dechazal2011 gives 78% accuracy and kappa 0.38, lower in the high-AHI group. No source shows consumer demand, willingness to pay, or insurance coverage: both assessed items are company assertions. T1 is favoured over T2 only because it has a mechanism and an existing dealer route; T2's sole assessed support (accuracy) does not bear on insurers. Demand is unknown.
justification.uncertain: Whether individual sleep-apnoea patients will pay a premium out of pocket: no assessed source shows demand or willingness to pay. resmed-pm-dechazal2011's 78% accuracy and kappa 0.38, lower in the high-AHI group, is a technical risk for the exact patients T1 targets. T2 (insurer-driven adoption) has no evidence insurers would cover the device. Challenge searches found no contradicting demand evidence. I rate both T1 and T2 uncertain, not likely.
justification.why_next: X1 separates T1 from T2 on willingness to pay: T1 predicts WTP at or above $150 and at least 30% intent among diagnosed patients (premium self-pay); T2 predicts WTP at or below $100 and at most 20% (insurance-dependent). Since no source yet shows demand, running X1 before committing funds is the bounded next step; clearing T1's threshold supports a consumer pilot, while T2's outcome means holding and re-examining B2B/insurer routes via resmed-pr-biancamed. Stated intentions can overstate demand, so X1 should capture deposits or pre-orders where feasible. The finish call therefore acts on X1.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for individuals with sleep apnea, leveraging ResMed’s non-contact technology and existing clinical validation. Begin with a limited pilot to test willingness to pay and purchase intent before full rollout.
arguments.target_customer: Consumers with sleep apnea who currently rely on clinic testing for diagnosis and monitoring.
arguments.value_proposition: A home sleep test device that uses non-contact technology to measure sleep and breathing, validated against polysomnography, offering convenience, accuracy, and the option of follow-up care and data analysis.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (or a similar test) to validate demand and willingness to pay. If thresholds are met, proceed to develop and pilot the consumer product; otherwise, conduct further market research.
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, actual willingness to pay, and the likelihood of insurance coverage for home sleep tests are uncertain. Evidence of consumer demand is limited to existing B2B sales and a single company claim about a non‑接触
would_change_if: If the willingness-to-pay survey shows WTP < $100 or purchase intent < 20% among sleep apnea patients, we would abandon consumer expansion and focus on B2B markets.
If new evidence shows that insurance coverage is widespread and affordable for home sleep tests, we would reconsider T2 as a viable route.
If a competitor launches a consumer‑focused home sleep test at a lower price, we would reassess the competitive landscape.

examples.review_note: A final recommendation should stay conditional when demand evidence is absent: do not commit to a consumer launch; favour the theory with a real mechanism and route (T1) while keeping both T1 and T2 uncertain; and gate investment on a bounded willingness-to-pay test with explicit thresholds that discriminates self-pay (WTP >= $150 / >= 30% intent) from insurance-dependent adoption (<= $100 / <= 20%). examples.question: It is March 2016. Should Embrace Innovations develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its infant-warming technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Parents of premature and low-birth-weight infants in low-resource settings will adopt a home infant warmer if it is priced below $100 and marketed as a life-saving medical device that reduces the risk of SIDS.
theories.T2: Parents of premature and low-birth-weight infants will adopt a home infant warmer if it is marketed as a fashion accessory and sold through trendy consumer channels, because they view infant care as a status symbol and are willing to pay a premium for design and brand.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest yet. Public sources show only company claims and hospital adoption, not that parents buy a home warmer. Hold investment until a bounded real-demand test — refundable deposits or pre-orders among parents of premature/low-birth-weight infants — shows meaningful purchase commitment. If it does, pursue the medical, low-cost positioning (T1), not a fashion proposition.
arguments.target_customer: Parents of premature and low-birth-weight infants in low-resource settings who lack reliable access to incubators and want a simple, low-cost warmer for home use.
arguments.value_proposition: A low-cost infant warmer positioned as a life-saving medical device that keeps babies from being too warm or too cold, a factor the company links to SIDS risk (embrace-her-sids).
arguments.next_action: Run a bounded deposit pilot (proposed): offer a refundable deposit for a home warmer to parents of premature/LBW infants at one low-resource hospital discharge; proceed only if ≥30% of eligible parents actually deposit.
arguments.uncertainty: Demand from individual buyers is unproven: embrace-ee-origin and embrace-her-sids are company claims; embrace-smg-launch shows hospital adoption, not consumer purchases. No purchase, conversion, affordability or financial data was found.
would_change_if: A deposit/pre-order pilot shows fewer than 30% (proposed threshold) of eligible parents actually commit — then keep the B2B focus and do not invest.
Independent evidence shows parents purchase a home warmer at scale, or that a different customer or use case drives stronger demand than low-resource LBW home use.

justification.learned: Embrace already sells to individuals: Little Lotus swaddles on its website, cut from $98 to $85 (embrace-cnbc-price, Feb 2016). The warmer began as a design challenge for premature/low-birth-weight infants where incubators are hard to obtain (embrace-ee-origin); the hospital-focused Embrace Nest launched in India in 2011 and is widely used (embrace-smg-launch). No source shows parents buying a home warmer; no sales data found. T1 (medical, low-cost) is favoured: origin and launch are medical/B2B, though that is capability/claim, not demand. T2 (fashion/status) has no real support; embrace-her-sids's SIDS claim is safety, not fashion demand.
justification.uncertain: Whether parents of premature/low-birth-weight infants would actually pay for a home warmer is unknown. embrace-ee-origin and embrace-her-sids are company claims; embrace-smg-launch shows hospital adoption, not consumer purchase. No source gives purchase intent, conversion, affordability, or repeat use. T2's status/fashion mechanism has no evidence.
justification.why_next: X1 is a messaging-only survey and would not separate willingness to pay from framing, so I do not recommend running it as-is. Instead act on T1 (supported by embrace-ee-origin and embrace-smg-launch): run a bounded real-demand pilot offering refundable deposits/pre-orders for a home warmer to parents of premature/LBW infants at a low-resource hospital discharge, varying medical vs fashion framing as a secondary factor but measuring actual deposits (proposed ≥30% commitment threshold) before any investment.

examples.question: Should Cotral Lab develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing hearing-protection offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Professional musicians will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a performanceenhancing tool that preserves sound quality while blocking noise, because they value accurate sound and are willing to pay a premium for a product that does not compromise their craft.
theories.T2: Sleep aid users will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a medical-grade solution that reduces sleep disruption caused by background noise, because they seek a product that addresses a specific health concern and are willing to pay for a solution that improves sleep quality.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to developing a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows manufacturing capability (ctl-filter, ctl-it1) but no consumer demand and a B2B route to market (ctl-channel). Validate a real consumer route and willingness to pay before investing.
arguments.target_customer: Unvalidated. Musicians are the least-weak hypothesis because an independent study and competitor products exist, but no source shows they would buy Cotral Lab's custom moulds.
arguments.value_proposition: Not yet validated. 'Performance-enhancing sound preservation' (T1) is weakened by bockstael-2015-looks, which found comfort and looks mattered more than sound quality.
arguments.next_action: Acting on ctl-channel's B2B finding, first confirm a consumer route to individual musicians, then run a deposit-backed pre-order test of a custom mould measuring real purchase intent, replacing X1's stated-intent survey.
arguments.uncertainty: Whether any consumer segment will pay a premium and whether Cotral Lab can reach individual buyers outside its employer channel (ctl-channel).
would_change_if: A deposit-backed test shows real consumer purchase intent at a price covering the custom mould.
Evidence shows musicians value comfort/looks over sound quality, requiring a revised proposition.
A viable consumer route beyond direct-to-employer channels is found.

justification.learned: Cotral Lab is the world's No.1 custom-moulded hearing protection maker (ctl-deal), distributing "primarily through direct channels to end-user companies" (ctl-channel), impressions "on-site" (ctl-onsite). Filters that "eliminate or lessen noise on specific frequencies" (ctl-filter) and wireless moulds (ctl-it1) are capability, not demand; no source shows consumer demand or willingness to pay. The independent study (bockstael-2015-looks) found appreciation "mainly depended on comfort and looks", sound differences "less noticeable", weakening T1. Competitors exist (minuendo-claim); T2 (sleep) has no independent evidence. T1 is favoured only as least-weak, on feasibility not demand.
justification.uncertain: Whether any consumer segment would actually pay a premium; whether Cotral Lab has a route to individual buyers, since its channel is B2B direct to employers (ctl-channel); and whether sound quality or comfort/looks drives musician adoption (bockstael-2015-looks vs T1). T2 rests only on capability claims (ctl-filter, ctl-onsite) with no independent demand evidence. Consumer demand remains unknown.
justification.why_next: The real gap is not which use case, but whether a consumer route and real willingness to pay exist. ctl-channel shows a B2B direct model, so any consumer proposition needs a new route. bockstael-2015-looks warns the musician pitch must test comfort/looks, not sound quality alone, so the stated-intent survey X1 is insufficient. The next action therefore acts on ctl-channel's route finding and replaces X1 with a real purchase-signal test.

examples.question: Should Sealed Air develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its Bubble Wrap brand? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated Bubble Wrap proposition for home moving because they value the sound and tactile experience of popping the wrap, and they seek a fun, stress‑reducing activity for moving tasks.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated Bubble Wrap proposition for small‑business packaging because they need lightweight, space‑saving protective material that reduces shipping costs and improves storage efficiency.

arguments.recommendation: Do not yet invest in a differentiated consumer proposition. Public evidence shows Bubble Wrap's pop/stress-relief appeal but no proof that consumers would buy or pay for a kit. Validate demand first with a bounded consequential test; develop the poppable moving-kit proposition (T1) only if consumers actually pay, and otherwise stay with B2B packaging.
arguments.target_customer: Individuals preparing home moves who value the pop and stress-relief of Bubble Wrap; this target is a hypothesis, as no source confirms they would purchase or pay a premium.
arguments.value_proposition: A branded, poppable Bubble Wrap moving kit that turns packing fragile items into a fun, stress-reducing experience, differentiated from generic cushioning by the iconic pop.
arguments.next_action: Run a 12-week, €20k consequential test: a landing page with paid pre-orders/deposits offering a poppable moving kit (T1) vs a compact pop-less small-business shipper (T2), measuring paid conversion, not stated intent.
arguments.uncertainty: Whether any consumer would actually pay: the only demand signals are brand affection (sealedair-ap-stress) and B2B efficiency claims (sealedair-fortune-ecom), not purchases.
would_change_if: Clear willingness to pay: the bounded test shows consumers place paid orders/deposits for a poppable moving kit above a minimum threshold, reversing 'do not invest' to 'develop T1'.
The compact pop-less small-business offer outperforms the moving kit on paid conversion, shifting the favoured theory to T2.
Neither offer generates paid demand, confirming continued B2B focus and no consumer expansion.

justification.learned: Public sources show Bubble Wrap's consumer pull is the pop/stress-relief experience (sealedair-ap-stress: "the stress reducer disguised as package cushioning"), and that losing the pop triggered anger (sealedair-cbc-anger, neutral on purchase). The redesigned wrap's space-saving appeal is B2B efficiency evidence aimed at online retailers (sealedair-fortune-ecom), the firm's best seller is foam rather than Bubble Wrap (sealedair-dz-foam), and sealedair-pr-markets lists only B2B end markets. No source shows willingness to pay or adopt a differentiated consumer kit. T1 is favoured only because it has the sole direct consumer-demand mechanism; it remains a hypothesis.
justification.uncertain: Actual demand is unknown: nothing measured purchase, willingness to pay, or repeat use for a consumer kit. It is unclear whether home moving (T1) or small-business packaging (T2) would convert, whether brand affection transfers to a purchasable product, and whether the segment is large enough to justify investment; sealedair-ap-stress and sealedair-cbc-anger show affection, not buying.
justification.why_next: The test in state (X1) varies only moving-vs-small-business wording, so it can capture stated intent but cannot separate real demand or the T1 vs T2 mechanisms. A bounded consequential test is needed before investing: offer both a poppable moving kit (T1) and a compact pop-less small-business shipper (T2) and measure paid pre-orders/deposits, not survey intent, so the two theories predict different conversion outcomes.

examples.question: Should Andis develop a further differentiated proposition for people who cut hair at home, beyond its existing at-home range, or concentrate on professional barbers and groomers? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Home users will adopt a differentiated at-home proposition if they perceive it as a premium, professional-quality experience that builds confidence and reduces salon visits.
theories.T2: Home users will adopt a differentiated at-home proposition if they perceive it as a convenient, time-saving solution that reduces the need for salon visits.

sources_read.andis-1997-home-kits: unknown (International Directory of Company Histories, Volume 85)

arguments.recommendation: Proceed cautiously with a further differentiated at-home proposition built on professional quality and confidence (T1), using Andis's existing home line and professional heritage — but do not scale before a behavioural test confirms willingness to pay. Concentrating on professional barbers and groomers remains the fallback if home users will not pay a premium.
arguments.target_customer: Home users who already cut hair at home and want professional-looking results without salon visits; a group that grew by over 6 million people after lockdowns (andis-wahl-6-million).
arguments.value_proposition: Professional-grade home kits drawing on '100 years of innovation in professional barbering' (andis-home-line), marketed for at-home confidence, with premium branding and performance claims rather than convenience-led features.
arguments.next_action: Run a bounded behavioural pilot (within €20k and 12 weeks): offer the existing home kit in 'professional quality' vs 'convenience' positions and capture deposits or real purchases, measuring take-up and price paid to separate T1 from T2.
arguments.uncertainty: Demand for a premium at-home proposition is unproven: no public source shows home users will pay a premium for professional quality (T1) or convenience (T2).
would_change_if: A deposit/purchase pilot shows no meaningful lift in take-up or willingness to pay for the professional-quality position (e.g., under 15% lift), redirecting resources toward professional barbers and groomers.
Independent evidence shows home users rank convenience or price saving above professional quality, contradicting T1 and favouring T2 or no expansion.

justification.learned: Andis already reaches individual buyers: its home grooming line is branded "Pro-Level Tools. At Home Confidence," built on "100 years of innovation in professional barbering" (andis-home-line), with kits at $24.99–$59.99 (andis-athome-prices). Market evidence: 6 million+ joined home haircutting after lockdowns and the clipper market rose 42% (andis-wahl-6-million); Wahl expects ~10% more to cut mostly at home than pre-pandemic (andis-wahl-10-percent). One buyer's ~$20 clippers "lasted me for five haircuts" (andis-attest-20-dollars). T1 (professional quality) is favoured over T2 (convenience), but support is mostly Andis's own claims; no source shows willingness to pay a premium.
justification.uncertain: The decisive fact is unknown: no public source shows home users' willingness to pay a premium for professional quality (T1) or convenience (T2). T1 rests on Andis's branding claim (andis-home-line) and one observation (andis-attest-20-dollars); T2 rests on overall growth (andis-wahl-6-million), not isolating convenience as the cause. Family-owned with non-public financials, so at-home margins and share are unverifiable.
justification.why_next: X1's conjoint varies only concept messaging and would measure stated preference, not demand, so it cannot safely separate T1 from T2. The bounded next step is a behavioural pilot: offer the existing at-home kit (andis-home-line) in "professional quality" versus "convenience" positions and capture refundable deposits or real purchases, measuring take-up and price paid within €20k and 12 weeks. This acts on T1 (professional quality) while letting T2 (convenience) show up in actual choices, not just survey answers.

examples.question: Should ZARGES develop a differentiated proposition for home users, beyond its existing ladder offering, or stay with professional buyers? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Home users will adopt ZARGES ladders if they perceive them as safety-critical tools for home improvement, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay premium prices.
theories.T2: Home users will adopt ZARGES ladders if they perceive them as premium, high-quality products that signal professional-grade reliability, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay premium prices.

arguments.recommendation: Do not launch a full home-user proposition yet. The evidence supports a safety-led home opportunity but not willingness to pay; ZARGES should test a safety-differentiated offer while keeping professional buyers as its core, committing only if home buyers pay a premium.
arguments.target_customer: DIY homeowners and farm users who undertake home improvement, where 97% of ladder injuries occur (zarges-neiss-home).
arguments.value_proposition: A safety-certified, professional-grade home ladder that differentiates from the 80%+ of telescopic ladders that fail minimum safety checks (zarges-telescopic-fail).
arguments.next_action: Run a small deposit-based pre-order test on ZARGES's consumer channel: offer a safety-certified home ladder at a premium vs an uncertified alternative and measure actual deposits/orders, separating T1 from T2.
arguments.uncertainty: No source shows home buyers will pay a premium for safety certification or ZARGES's current consumer reach; demand is unproven despite the 97% home-injury and 80%+ failure figures.
would_change_if: A real-purchase test shows safety-certified ZARGES ladders convert no better at a premium than lower-priced alternatives
ZARGES's existing consumer reach proves negligible or costly to build

justification.learned: Public sources confirm ZARGES already lists ladders for "home and garden" (zarges-catalogue-home), so it has some consumer-facing offering. Independent studies show a home-segment safety problem: 97% of ladder injuries occurred in non-occupational settings (zarges-neiss-home), and 80%+ of telescopic ladders failed minimum safety checks (zarges-telescopic-fail), with only 5 of 12 passing EN131 rigidity (zarges-hk-rigidity). This favours T1 (safety-driven demand) over T2 (premium-branding demand): the safety mechanism has corroborating market evidence, while T2's brand-prestige mechanism has none. No source, however, shows home buyers will pay a premium, so demand is not yet proven.
justification.uncertain: Willingness to pay is unknown. The studies show a safety problem exists (zarges-neiss-home, zarges-telescopic-fail, zarges-hk-rigidity) but not that homeowners will pay more for a certified ladder, nor ZARGES's current consumer reach or price sensitivity. T1 is plausible on mechanism, but premium demand is unverified.
justification.why_next: T1 and T2 differ only in what drives a home buyer to pay a premium: safety (T1) versus brand prestige (T2). The proposed test X1 measures only survey intent, so I rely on T1 and T2 and act on T1 by proposing a bounded step that observes real purchasing behaviour (deposits/orders), which can separate the two mechanisms.

arguments.target_customer: Homeowners who undertake DIY home improvement and are safety-conscious, particularly those who have experienced ladder-related injuries or are aware of safety standards.
arguments.value_proposition: Safety-certified ladders that meet European standards (EN131) and are marketed as reliable, injury‑preventing tools, positioned at a premium price point (e.g., €20 above generic ladders).

examples.question: It is March 2016. Should Embrace Innovations develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its infant-warming technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Parents of low‑birth‑weight infants will adopt a home‑use infant warmer if they perceive it as a medical necessity that reduces the risk of SIDS and is affordable, because they are willing to pay a premium for a product that addresses a serious health concern.
theories.T2: Parents of low‑birth‑weight infants will adopt a home‑use infant warmer if they perceive it as a convenient, affordable way to monitor their baby’s temperature and health at home, because they value time‑saving and ease of use, and are willing to pay a price that reflects the convenience.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest yet. The only support for a consumer proposition is Embrace's own SIDS claim (embrace-her-sids), which shows positioning feasibility but not demand. Validate demand with a bounded pre-order/deposit test; commit to a consumer launch only if parents demonstrably pay.
arguments.target_customer: Parents of premature or low-birth-weight infants who would warm and monitor a baby at home — a segment whose demand is unproven and should be treated as a hypothesis.
arguments.value_proposition: A home-use infant warmer positioned as reducing SIDS risk and keeping babies at a safe temperature — a benefit Embrace asserts (embrace-her-sids) but has not independently verified.
arguments.next_action: Run a 12-week, €20,000 deposit-based pre-order test (landing page with refundable deposit) comparing the T1 SIDS/medical-necessity and T2 convenience propositions, using deposit conversion as the primary behavioural measure.
arguments.uncertainty: Whether parents will actually pay, and whether the SIDS-reduction benefit is real; the dossier has no independent demand, sales or financial data.
would_change_if: Deposits or pre-orders clearing a pre-set conversion threshold would reverse this to invest
A test showing no meaningful deposits under either T1 or T2 would strengthen the case for staying B2B/no expansion

justification.learned: Only two of six sources bear on the theories. embrace-her-sids, a company assertion, is the sole support for T1: Embrace "claim their product may even reduce the risk of SIDS" — a positioning/benefit claim, not proof parents will buy. embrace-ee-origin is neutral for T2 and never addresses convenience. No source shows actual consumer demand, willingness to pay, or market size for a home warmer. embrace-cnbc-price shows a consumer product already exists (Little Lotus swaddles, $85–98), but it is a swaddle, not the warmer; embrace-gsb-investors flags investor pressure against small markets. Demand is therefore unknown.
justification.uncertain: Whether parents of low-birth-weight infants would actually pay for a home-use warmer, and whether T1 (medical necessity/SIDS risk) or T2 (convenience/time-saving monitoring) drives the purchase. The SIDS benefit rests only on Embrace's own claim (embrace-her-sids); no independent study validates it and the dossier holds no sales or financial data. Both mechanisms lack direct demand evidence.
justification.why_next: Evidence weakly favours T1 over T2 — T1 has one supportive (company) claim, T2 none, but a company claim cannot justify investment. I would replace X1's stated-intent survey with a bounded deposit-based pre-order test that separates T1 and T2 by measuring consequential behaviour (refundable deposits) under the SIDS/medical-necessity versus convenience propositions. Act on T1 and T2.

arguments.target_customer: Parents of premature or low-birth-weight infants who need additional home monitoring and are willing to pay a premium for a product that addresses a serious health concern.
arguments.value_proposition: A home infant warmer that provides safe, controlled warming and monitoring, backed by medical claims of reduced SIDS risk, sold at a premium price that reflects the health benefit and convenience of home use.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Parent Preference Survey (300 parents, 8 weeks, €15,000) to test whether medical necessity drives purchase intent. Use the results to decide whether to proceed with a full consumer launch or refine the proposition.
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and willingness to pay a premium for medical necessity are uncertain. Evidence from the survey will resolve whether convenience (T2) or medical necessity (T1) is the primary driver.
would_change_if: If the survey shows convenience ranking higher than medical necessity with a ≥2-point difference, we would shift focus to a convenience‑focused proposition and lower the price point.

examples.question: It is early 2009. Should Aspen Aerogels develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its flexible aerogel blanket insulation? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Residential homeowners will adopt Aspen Aerogels flexible aerogel blanket insulation if they perceive it as a premium, high-performance product that provides superior thermal comfort and durability compared to conventional insulation.
theories.T2: Homeowners will adopt Aspen Aerogels flexible aerogel blanket insulation if they perceive it as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces energy consumption and carbon footprint, leveraging the material’s proven thermal performance.

arguments.quote: Toasty Feet are insulated with Aerogel, which was developed by Aspen Aerogels for NASA, and is claimed to have the highest thermal insulation value of any solid material available.
arguments.does_not_show: Shows aerogel's presence in a consumer product and a NASA/high-performance quality signal; it cannot show that homeowners would buy or pay a premium for Aspen's blanket insulation, or any purchasing behaviour.

justification.learned: Read aspen-bpl-toasty (2007), aspen-ft-consumers (2022), aspen-rc-ipo (2013). Only aspen-bpl-toasty predates the decision date. It shows aerogel had already reached a consumer product (Toasty Feet insoles) and carried a "developed by Aspen Aerogels for NASA" / "highest thermal insulation" framing — the closest pre-2009 evidence for T1's premium-performance quality-signal assumption. The 2022 review and 2013 IPO withdrawal are post-decision and can be context, not 2009 knowledge.
justification.uncertain: No source yet shows homeowner demand for aerogel blanket insulation, willingness to pay a premium, or actual purchase behaviour. aspen-ft-consumers notes consumers struggled to differentiate aerogel clothing from conventional insulation, but it is not knowable in 2009. T2's sustainability motivation has not yet been weighed against any source.
justification.why_next: Weigh aspen-bpl-toasty against T1 because it is the only pre-decision source touching the consumer-facing NASA/performance positioning T1 depends on. It can bear on feasibility and positioning, but the assessment must not treat that as proof of homeowner demand, so I will separate capability from purchasing behaviour in the call.

examples.question: Should ARRI develop a differentiated proposition of its own for individual creators, beyond its professional cinema range and its smartphone partnership, or keep its consumer presence to partners? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Individual creators will adopt ARRI products if they perceive the brand as a professional standard and are willing to pay a premium for reliability and image quality.
theories.T2: Individual creators will adopt ARRI products if they perceive the brand as a professional standard and are willing to pay a premium for reliability and image quality, but will also be attracted by the smartphone partnership that already provides them with a professional-grade camera and creative control.

arguments.quote: For most filmmakers, ARRI has always been a brand they use rather than a brand they own. ALEXA cameras sit at the top of the professional cinema market, commonly purchased by rental houses, studios, and production companies rather than individual creators.
arguments.does_not_show: This shows the current ownership structure, not that creators would switch to buying or pay a premium; it offers no willingness-to-pay or purchase-intent evidence.

justification.learned: Sources show ARRI is premium and cinema-centric: a new $55,000 Alexa 35 Xtreme (arri-alexa-price), 150 job cuts and two site closures amid production decline (arri-cined-challenges), and ARRI's own statement that its core focus stays "high-end cinema and live entertainment" (arri-core-focus). ARRI also calls the Honor Robot Phone a milestone in its "expansion into Content Creation" (arri-honor-milestone). The key market-structure fact (arri-ymc-use-not-own) is that filmmakers use ARRI rather than own it, with ALEXAs bought by rental houses/studios rather than individual creators.
justification.uncertain: No source yet shows individual-creator demand, willingness to pay a premium, or intent to switch from rental to purchase; T1 and T2 still rest on assumptions, not observed demand. arri-core-focus suggests ARRI's own stated core focus is high-end cinema, which cuts against direct consumer expansion, while arri-honor-milestone hints at consumer reach only through a partner.
justification.why_next: Weigh arri-ymc-use-not-own against T1 because it bears directly on T1's assumption that creators currently rely on rental/use-not-own, the premise any shift-to-purchase claim depends on. The assess_evidence call records it as market_fact and states what it cannot show (willingness to pay or purchase intent), then later sources can be weighed against T2.

examples.question: It is mid-2014. Should ResMed develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its non-contact sleep-sensing technology and sleep-medicine expertise? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Individuals with sleep apnoea will adopt a home sleep test device if they perceive it as convenient and accurate, and if they are willing to pay a premium for non-contact technology that avoids the need for clinic visits.
theories.T2: Insurance companies will cover home sleep tests if they are validated against polysomnography and demonstrate clinical efficacy, leading consumers to adopt home testing because they avoid clinic visits and reduce out-of-pocket costs.

arguments.quote: The S+ will be available for the suggested retail price of $149.99 at Bed Bath & Beyond® stores beginning in mid-October and online at mysplus.com .
arguments.does_not_show: It does not show that any consumer adopted the S+, was willing to pay $149.99, or expressed purchase intent; a launch announcement is the company's plan and pricing, not demand.

justification.learned: ResMed's 10-K says it markets "primarily to home healthcare dealers and to sleep clinics" (resmed-10k-clinics), a B2B route, not individuals. BiancaMed PR (resmed-pr-biancamed) shows a non-contact sensor marketed for "home and hospital"—a capability claim. The S+ PR (resmed-pr-splus) is the only consumer-facing source: $149.99 at Bed Bath & Beyond and online. All three are company claims; none is customer or independent demand evidence. resmed-pr-splus is right to weigh against T1 because T1 is about consumer adoption and willingness to pay, and this is the only source bearing on consumer price and route.
justification.uncertain: Whether sleep apnoea patients actually want, trust, or will pay a premium for non-contact home sensing. A $149.99 list price is the company's chosen price, not evidence that consumers will pay it. No source so far shows purchase intent, sales, repeat use, or independent demand. Whether insurance coverage (T2) would shift adoption or price sensitivity is also unresolved.
justification.why_next: Weigh resmed-pr-splus against T1: it bears on feasibility and value-capture design (a premium price and consumer channel exist) but cannot establish the adoption/willingness-to-pay mechanism T1 claims. After this, find independent or customer-side evidence bearing on T2 (insurance-driven adoption) and challenge T1's demand assumption.

examples.question: It is 1983. Should Mag Instrument develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its machined anodized-aluminium flashlights? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Civilians will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they perceive the Maglite as a status symbol and a symbol of professional reliability, leading them to purchase multiple units for personal use.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they need reliable, high‑performance flashlights for outdoor recreation and home safety, and they are willing to pay a premium for durability and professional‑grade features.

arguments.quote: The Maglite is a powerful and durable flashlight and for many years was the standard issued gear used by police officers in the USA.
arguments.does_not_show: It does not show that this police reputation transferred to civilians, that civilians saw it as a status symbol, or that they would pay a premium or buy multiple units.

justification.learned: Read mag-amw-standard (Wikipedia) showing the Maglite was 'standard issued gear used by police officers'; mag-fu-civilians and mag-fu-magcharger (FundingUniverse) showing civilian-appeal design intent and the 1982 Mag Charger; and mag-pat2-cheaper (patent) showing a simpler, cheaper-to-make design. T1 (status/professional reliability) and T2 (outdoor/home-safety functional need) are open. No source yet shows civilian demand, willingness to pay, or specific use-case purchases. mag-amw-standard adds third-party confirmation of the police-standard reputation T1 assumes transfers to civilians; it is the right source to weigh now because it is the only non-company source bearing on T1's premise.

examples.question: Should Hilti develop a differentiated proposition for home users or hobbyists, beyond its existing professional offering, or leave that market alone? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Homeowners and hobbyists will adopt Hilti tools if they perceive them as reliable and professional-grade, and are willing to pay a premium for durability.
theories.T2: Homeowners and hobbyists will adopt Hilti tools if they perceive them as reliable and professional-grade, and are willing to pay a premium for durability, but will also be sensitive to price and seek the best value.

sources_read.hilti-consumer-market-size: unknown (written while the COVID-19 pandemic was ongoing)
sources_read.hilti-consumers-price-sensitive: unknown (written while the COVID-19 pandemic was ongoing)

arguments.quote: Unlike professionals, however – who are generally more willing to pay a premium for better performing and longer lasting power tools – most consumers are very price sensitive when it comes to these products, often opting for less costly imports over expensive professional-grade models.
arguments.does_not_show: It cannot show what Hilti homeowners specifically would do, whether Hilti's brand changes this pattern, or actual purchase behavior; it is an industry-level characterization of consumers generally.

justification.learned: Read so far: Hilti is B2B with a direct sales model (hilti-b2b-reach, hilti-direct-model). The DIY market is about half the professional market (hilti-consumer-market-size) and homeowners are 70% of power tool purchasers (hilti-homeowners-share), but price is the top driver and most purchases are in-store (hilti-price-driver). Consumers are very price sensitive, opting for cheaper imports over professional-grade models (hilti-consumers-price-sensitive). T1 and T2 differ only on price sensitivity, so hilti-consumers-price-sensitive is the right source to weigh now because it discriminates willingness to pay a premium.
justification.uncertain: No source read yet shows Hilti-specific demand, purchase intent, or actual behavior among homeowners/hobbyists. The 70% homeowner share is volume, not evidence of premium willingness. Whether Hilti's brand reputation could override the general consumer price sensitivity remains unknown from the evidence read.
justification.why_next: Weigh hilti-consumers-price-sensitive against T1; if it contradicts T1's premium-willingness assumption, T2 is better supported. examples.question: Should ARRI develop a differentiated proposition of its own for individual creators, beyond its professional cinema range and its smartphone partnership, or keep its consumer presence to partners? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Individual creators will adopt ARRI products if they perceive them as a status symbol and a differentiator for their work, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.
theories.T2: Individual creators will adopt ARRI products if they perceive them as a necessary tool for their craft, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when priced competitively.

arguments.quote: For most filmmakers, ARRI has always been a brand they use rather than a brand they own. ALEXA cameras sit at the top of the professional cinema market, commonly purchased by rental houses, studios, and production companies rather than individual creators.
arguments.does_not_show: This describes who currently buys ARRI (rental houses, studios), not why individual creators would buy it; it cannot show status signaling drives adoption or willingness to pay.

S5: ARRI is "a brand they use rather than a brand they own... commonly purchased by rental houses, studios, and production companies rather than individual creators." Theories: T1 (status symbol) and T2 (necessary tool at competitive pricing). No individual-creator demand or willingness-to-pay data found.
justification.uncertain: Whether individual creators would buy ARRI at all, and whether status (T1) or necessity (T2) would drive adoption, is unmeasured. S5 shows creators currently use rather than own ARRI, but gives no motivation data; S4 is a company assertion about "creative control" and access, not evidence of demand or willingness to pay.
justification.why_next: Weigh S5 (arri-ymc-use-not-own) against T1 next: it is the only source read that speaks directly to individual creators' relationship with ARRI ownership, so it is the right one to test T1's status-symbol assumption. The assessment must stay honest — S5 describes current ownership structure, not creators' purchase motivation, so it cannot confirm T1.

examples.question: It is March 1991. Should Intel Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its microprocessors? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Home networking will create a demand for Intel microprocessors, and if Intel can differentiate its chips for this use case, it can capture premium pricing.
theories.T2: Gamers will adopt Intel microprocessors if they offer superior gaming performance, and if Intel can differentiate its chips for gaming, it can capture premium pricing from this segment.

arguments.quote: The consumer is the end-user of the ingredient, but is not part of the buying decision for the component, as this is up to the producer of the end product.
arguments.does_not_show: It cannot show whether households want home networking in 1991, whether OEMs would pick Intel for a networking chip, or whether consumers would pay more for the finished product; it only describes the general component-buying structure.

justification.learned: Read intel-court-oem, intel-csm-nocare, intel-ib-buyer. intel-court-oem shows Intel's own litigation treats OEMs, not consumers, as the relevant buyers for 386 perception: 'one composed of Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) who purchase microprocessors for inclusion as component parts.' intel-csm-nocare quotes an OEM product manager: 'I don't think anyone's going to care.' intel-ib-buyer states the ingredient-branding structure: consumers are end-users but not part of the component buying decision. This bears on T1's value-capture premise, which assumes consumers choose and pay a premium for Intel networking chips.

examples.question: It is late 2012. Should Cree, Inc. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its high-brightness LED chips and LED lighting technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt LED bulbs if they are priced low enough to be competitive with incandescent bulbs, because price is the primary barrier to switching.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt LED bulbs if they perceive them as a premium product offering superior color quality and design, because they value aesthetic and functional differentiation.

arguments.quote: According to retailers, consumers are embracing LEDs, which were the focus of the prize, and CFLs, or compact fluorescent lights, faster than many in the industry expected.
arguments.does_not_show: This shows adoption was occurring, but it says nothing about why; it does not establish that price is the primary barrier, so it leaves T1's causal claim unresolved.

justification.learned: So far the dossier shows Cree had some pre-2012 consumer reach (cree-pr-ecosmart: a Home Depot EcoSmart downlight "retails for less than $50"), and one independent, pre-decision market observation (cree-bdn-embracing) that retailers said consumers were adopting LEDs and CFLs faster than expected. The post-2012 sources (cree-ledp-reason, cree-wiki-first) describe 2013 events and cannot inform a late-2012 decision. Two rival mechanisms are open: T1 (price is the primary barrier to switching) and T2 (premium color/design drives adoption).

justification.why_next: Weigh cree-bdn-embracing against T1 now: it is the only independent, pre-decision observation about consumer behaviour in the dossier, so it is the right source to test whether any adoption evidence exists. examples.question: It is late 2005. Should OraSure Technologies develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its rapid oral-fluid HIV antibody test for clinics and public-health programmes? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Individuals will adopt an at-home HIV test if they view it as a private, discreet health decision, leading to purchase even without clinic referral.
theories.T2: Individuals will adopt an at-home HIV test if they view it as a convenient, low‑cost health monitoring tool, leading to purchase even without clinic referral.

arguments.quote: The original version of this rapid test -- the OraQuick Rapid HIV-1/2 Antibody Test, manufactured by OraSure Technologies, Inc., Bethlehem , Pa. -- was approved November 7, 2002 for detection of antibody to HIV-1 in blood.
arguments.does_not_show: This shows regulatory clearance for a blood-based rapid test; it cannot show consumers will buy an oral-fluid home test for privacy or any demand.

justification.learned: Sources so far: orasure-fda04-approval (FDA approval of OraQuick rapid HIV-1/2 blood test, 2002), orasure-k023487-db (a 510(k) for a wart-removal device), and orasure-nbc12-retail (a 2012 company claim about at-home retail availability, after the 2005 decision date). Two theories are open: T1 (privacy-driven adoption) and T2 (convenience/cost-driven adoption). No source yet shows individual-buyer demand or willingness to pay. The FDA source is the right one to weigh: it is the only source on the regulatory feasibility of the rapid HIV test that T1 and T2 presuppose; the 510(k) is unrelated and the 2012 item is post-decision and a company claim.
justification.uncertain: Whether late-2005 evidence shows consumer demand for an at-home oral-fluid HIV test is unknown. orasure-fda04-approval concerns regulatory clearance, not demand; orasure-nbc12-retail is a 2012 company assertion and cannot be used to infer 2005 demand; orasure-k023487-db is about wart removal and is irrelevant. Neither T1's privacy mechanism nor T2's convenience/cost mechanism yet has customer_observation or independent_study support.
justification.why_next: Weigh orasure-fda04-approval against T1 as neutral: it establishes regulatory feasibility but not the privacy-driven adoption T1 claims. Then use remaining searches to find customer_observation or independent_study evidence on home HIV testing attitudes (privacy vs convenience), and run challenge_theory on T1 to look for contradicting evidence before proposing a test that would separate T1 from T2.

examples.question: It is 2014. Should Grundéns develop a differentiated proposition for recreational anglers, building on its commercial fishing raingear? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Recreational anglers will adopt Grundéns raingear because they value durability and professional-grade performance, and they are willing to pay a premium for gear that keeps them dry and comfortable during extended fishing sessions.
theories.T2: Recreational anglers will adopt Grundéns raingear because they value brand recognition and the perceived prestige of using a professional‑grade fishing brand, and they are willing to pay a premium for that association.

arguments.quote: The Herkules 16 bibs were crafted to keep commercial fishermen dry and comfortable through the long hours your captain may throw at you.
arguments.does_not_show: It shows the bibs are designed for long-hour durability and comfort in commercial fishing; it does not show recreational anglers value these attributes, would pay a premium, or would buy.

justification.learned: T1 (durability/professional performance motive) and T2 (brand prestige motive) are both open. Read sources include company claims (grundens-ai-us, grundens-oia-commitment, grundens-sgb-restaurants, grundens-sgb-versatility) and third-party/trade observations (grundens-nf-herkules, grundens-sgb-footwear, grundens-tot-channel, grundens-wiki-churn). grundens-nf-herkules is the only non-company description of the durability/comfort attribute that T1 says drives adoption; it is aimed at commercial fishermen. grundens-tot-channel shows a sportfishing line launched in 2016, after the 2014 question. grundens-wiki-churn shows participation churn (9.4M started, 9.1M stopped), not purchase behaviour.
justification.uncertain: No source read shows why recreational anglers buy or that they would pay a premium. The durability evidence (grundens-nf-herkules) concerns commercial use, not recreational motivation. Company claims (grundens-sgb-versatility, grundens-oia-commitment) are self-serving and post-2014. Recreational demand for a differentiated Grundéns proposition remains unknown.
justification.why_next: Weigh grundens-nf-herkules against T1: it is the only independent description of the durability/comfort capability T1's mechanism assumes, so it is the right source to test whether that premise has any support, while keeping capability distinct from recreational demand.

examples.question: It is 1888. Should S.L. Allen & Co. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its farm-implement manufacturing? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Individual gardeners and hobby farmers will adopt a differentiated seed drill for small plots because they need affordable, easy-to-use tools for home gardening and will purchase from a manufacturer that provides direct retail and after‑sale service.

arguments.claim: Commercial market gardeners and small-plot vegetable growers will adopt a compact seed drill as a business input because it can raise per-acre yield and planting precision, and they will pay a premium only if the tool is sold through the implement and seed dealers they already buy from.
arguments.who_benefits: Market gardeners who sell produce gain output and profit; Allen captures margin through its existing dealer channels instead of building a direct retail and service network.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: These growers buy implements as production inputs and judge purchases by return on investment, so they change behaviour when a tool demonstrably improves planting precision and yield per acre, not because it eases household gardening.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Allen sells through existing implement and seed-catalog dealers at a premium justified by yield gains, earning margin on unit volume without the cost of a new direct-retail or after-sale service operation.
assumptions: Commercial small-plot growers are numerous enough and have cash flow to invest in a drill.
Growers can observe or trust claimed yield and precision gains.
Allen's existing implement and seed dealers already reach these buyers.
A compact drill actually improves planting precision enough to affect yield.
predictions: When surveyed, commercial market gardeners express higher purchase intent for a compact drill than home hobby gardeners do.
Purchase intent rises when the offer emphasizes yield per acre, whereas T1 predicts it rises on an ease/convenience pitch.
Commercial buyers choose existing implement dealers over a new direct retail channel.

justification.learned: Read: allen-uspto-firm (Allen limited to agricultural implements/machinery for its first two decades), allen-uspto-components (workers already had the skills/machinery), allen-uspto-seasonal and allen-wp-slowseason (demand unpredictable; workers idle in summer). Only T1 exists: home-gardener adoption via convenience/labor-saving and direct retail+service. Last two calls refused because the second add_theory duplicated T1: "you already have that theory. A new theory must give a different causal explanation." Unread: allen-uspto-adreach, allen-uspto-rehire.
justification.uncertain: How far Allen already reaches individual buyers is still unknown because allen-uspto-adreach is unread; no financial data is in the dossier; and there is no evidence yet on whether home hobbyists or commercial small growers would actually pay. T1 remains an untested hypothesis with no assessed evidence.
justification.why_next: The theories stage requires a second theory with a different causal explanation than T1. I will add T2, which names a different cause (commercial market gardeners buying a drill as a yield/profit business input through existing dealers) rather than T1's home-convenience and direct-retail cause, so the two theories predict different buyers, different purchase triggers, and different channels.

examples.question: It is 2014. Should Grundéns develop a differentiated proposition for recreational anglers, building on its commercial fishing raingear? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Recreational anglers buy raingear to solve the same core problem as commercial fishermen — staying dry in sustained wet conditions — so gear built for commercial fishing transfers to recreational use without angler-specific redesign; anglers will adopt existing Grundéns gear, and Grundéns captures value through premium pricing on the unmodified product.
arguments.who_benefits: Recreational anglers who currently buy cheap or generic raingear and value reliable dryness over mobility or styling.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: They switch because commercial-grade PVC keeps them dry longer in real fishing conditions, so the functional benefit transfers directly with no need for angler-specific features.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Grundéns sells its existing commercial line to anglers at a premium through new or existing retail, avoiding redesign and tooling cost.
assumptions: Anglers' dominant need is staying dry, not comfort, mobility or aesthetics
Existing commercial gear can reach anglers without modification (sizing, fit, retail access)
Anglers perceive Grundéns as available and worth its price
predictions: Anglers shown existing Grundéns gear express purchase intent similar to or higher than for a redesigned angler version
Unmodified gear sells to anglers at least as well as differentiated gear in a comparable retail test
Few angler returns cite fit or comfort as the reason

examples.question: It is early 2003. Should Quantum Devices, Inc. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its high-intensity LED light sources for medical research and military first aid? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: LED light therapy is adopted mainly when a clinician validates it as a treatment for a diagnosed condition (e.g., oral mucositis or slow-healing wounds); patients do not self-diagnose and self-treat at home, so in 2003 demand flows through hospitals, clinics, and researchers rather than individual consumers.
arguments.who_benefits: Patients with diagnosed conditions (oral mucositis, wounds) and the clinicians who treat them.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Adoption requires a diagnostic context and professional endorsement; patients follow clinician recommendations instead of buying unproven home devices.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Quantum Devices captures value by selling medically positioned devices to hospitals, clinics, and research institutions at premium medical-equipment prices.
assumptions: Clinical evidence is preliminary in 2003, so institutions rather than consumers make purchases.
The company's existing route to market is institutional/B2B.
Consumers have no reason to self-diagnose and self-treat with LED light.
predictions: Observed buyers of Quantum Devices LED units in 2003 would be hospitals, clinics, and research institutions, not individual households.
Consumer retail channels would show near-zero willingness to pay absent clinical endorsement.

justification.learned: Sources read so far: FDA 510(k) K032229 cleared the QUANTUM WARP 10 as an infrared therapeutic-heating device (qdi-fda-k032229); FTC's 1999 Operation Cure.All shows regulatory risk for unsubstantiated consumer health claims (qdi-ftc-cureall); a Dec 2002 mucositis study found LED therapy "appears useful" but "more studies are needed" (qdi-pm-mucositis2002). No theories exist yet (theories: {}).
justification.uncertain: Whether any individual buyers already purchase Quantum Devices products, what demand was knowable by early 2003, and which causal mechanism would drive value for a consumer proposition (clinical adoption vs. consumer convenience vs. regulatory trust). The last calls were refused because they repeated the same search, "LED therapy home market 2003", three times.

examples.question: Should Festool develop a differentiated proposition for hobbyist woodworkers, beyond its existing offering, or keep a single range for all buyers? What evidence would justify either choice?

arguments.claim: Hobbyist woodworkers buy Festool because owning the same tools professionals use signals competence and serious intent; a separate, visibly lower-tier hobbyist range would strip away that status signal and reduce their willingness to pay, so a single premium range protects hobbyist demand.
arguments.who_benefits: Hobbyists seeking a professional identity, and Festool through preserved premium pricing.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: The purchase is motivated by identity, not only function. If the product is relabelled as hobby-grade, it no longer confers professional status, so hobbyists stop paying premium prices, defer purchase, or buy the pro line anyway.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Festool keeps one premium line, sells at high margin to both segments, and avoids the tooling, inventory and marketing cost of a second lower-priced line.
assumptions: Hobbyists primarily value Festool for professional-grade status, not only performance or system features.
A lower-priced hobby line would be visibly distinguishable from the pro line.
Hobbyists currently pay full price despite the hobbyist segment growing slower than professional.
predictions: In a survey or conjoint, hobbyists rate 'same tools the pros use' as a top purchase driver over lower price.
Shown a hypothetical 'Festool Hobby' line at ~30% lower price, hobbyists' stated purchase intent does not rise versus the existing line.
Under a single range, hobbyist repeat-purchase and premium willingness-to-pay remain stable.

justification.learned: From the three Core77 excerpts (festool-hobby-growth, festool-mix, festool-woodcraft-origin), Festool's US buyer mix is now roughly 60% professional / 40% hobbyist, down from ~70% hobbyist in 2004-05, and the professional segment grows faster than the hobbyist segment. Hobbyist draw was partly driven by limited distribution through Woodcraft, a dealer that caters to hobbyists. No sources yet show why hobbyists buy, whether they are price-sensitive, or whether a differentiated proposition would change their behaviour. The last two calls were refused because the same search (Festool hobbyist price) had already been run; no new search results exist to read.
justification.uncertain: It is unknown whether hobbyists buy Festool for professional-grade identity, for system benefits, or because dealers like Woodcraft educate and guide them. There is no evidence on hobbyist price sensitivity, willingness to pay, or repeat behaviour, and no theories have been added yet. Festool's actual reach to individual buyers beyond this dealer mix remains undiscovered.
justification.why_next: The stage requires at least two causal theories, and none exist yet. I am adding the first theory (T1) on identity/aspiration, which predicts a single range; rival theories (price sensitivity, channel/guidance) will be added next with different causes.

examples.question: It is mid-2015. Should Illumina develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its DNA sequencing and genotyping technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Consumers buy DNA tests mainly when results are personally actionable for their health, not raw data or novelty. A consumer proposition therefore succeeds only if it delivers medically credible, FDA-accepted health information.
arguments.who_benefits: Health-conscious adults with family disease history or wellness concerns who lack easy access to clinical genetic screening.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Raw or unvalidated results feel risky and useless, so they abstain; clinically meaningful, FDA-accepted health results give them a reason to pay, act, and return.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Illumina earns sequencing volume and premium pricing by supplying a validated health-grade pipeline that third-party app partners need to offer credible results.
assumptions: Regulatory path for health claims is feasible and affordable
Consumers understand and act on health-risk results
App partners can build FDA-accepted health apps on Helix
predictions: Buyers pay more for and more often choose medically actionable health tests than ancestry/entertainment tests
Health-framed apps generate more repeat engagement than novelty apps
Demand concentrates where clinical/medical framing is present

justification.learned: Illumina is a San Diego sequencing/genotyping maker that has "mostly focused on catering to scientists and medical researchers" (illumina-kpbs-pivot), so it does not yet reach individual buyers directly. In Aug 2015 it formed Helix as a sequencing/database platform for third-party consumer apps (illumina-pr-helix). DTC genetic testing is dominated by 23andMe (illumina-kpbs-pivot), and since 2010 the FDA has treated genetic tests as medical devices requiring approval, writing to both 23andMe and Illumina (illumina-wiki-fda2010). No source yet shows consumer demand or willingness to pay. Two sources remain unread (illumina-pr-about, illumina-pr-dilutive).
justification.uncertain: Whether consumers buy for medical/actionable health value vs ancestry/identity, and whether Illumina captures value directly or only as a supplier. Demand and willingness to pay are still unknown. The unread sources may clarify Illumina's existing consumer reach and the financial impact of Helix.
justification.why_next: The stage requires at least two theories but none exist yet (0 of 2). I am adding the first causal theory of consumer demand now, grounded in the FDA/medical-device history (illumina-wiki-fda2010) and the Helix third-party-app structure (illumina-pr-helix); next I will read the unread sources and add a rival theory with a different cause.

examples.question: It is May 2026. Should Nilfisk develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its professional cleaning machines? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt Nilfisk vacuum cleaners if they perceive the brand as a premium, professional-grade product that delivers superior cleaning performance, because they value quality and are willing to pay a premium for it.

arguments.claim: Household vacuum buyers choose among established consumer brands at retail mainly on price, convenience and peer reviews; they see 'professional-grade' as irrelevant to home cleaning, so Nilfisk will convert consumers only at price parity and strong retail presence, not through a premium differentiated proposition.
arguments.who_benefits: Consumers who want an adequate, affordable vacuum with low shopping effort, and Nilfisk only if it wins volume through Freudenberg's consumer retail channels.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers switch when a Nilfisk model is cheaper than or equal to the familiar brand at the store or site where they already shop; professional credentials alone do not change their routine purchase behaviour.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Nilfisk captures value through retail volume and shelf presence under Freudenberg's consumer distribution, at mainstream rather than premium margins.
assumptions: Consumers treat home and professional cleaning as different tasks and discount professional branding for the home.
Nilfisk has low unaided brand awareness among household buyers.
Distribution and shelf placement, not performance messaging, are the binding constraint on consumer conversion.
predictions: In a forced-choice purchase-intent test, a Nilfisk vacuum priced 20% above a comparable generic model shows no more than a 5-percentage-point advantage over the generic, versus T1's predicted 15+ points.
At price parity with an established consumer brand, Nilfisk conversion is driven by where the product is placed, not by professional-grade claims.

justification.learned: Sources read so far (nilfisk-2025-split, nilfisk-wiki-consumer, nilfisk-accc-overlap, nilfisk-2026-standalone, nilfisk-fhcs-about) establish that Nilfisk already sells some consumer vacuum cleaners and high-pressure cleaners, but over 90% of sales are to professionals, and the ACCC determination describes Nilfisk as "largely for commercial use". The Freudenberg sources show a new consumer-products parent, but they are company claims about capability, not evidence of consumer demand. One theory (T1) exists, positing that a premium professional-grade positioning drives consumer adoption; my second add_theory call was refused because it duplicated T1 instead of giving a different cause.
justification.uncertain: Whether household buyers actually want a Nilfisk consumer proposition, whether they would pay a premium, and whether "professional-grade" positioning transfers to home use. No source read so far shows independent consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive positioning, so demand remains unknown.
justification.why_next: The next required step is a second causal theory that rivals T1 rather than repeating it. I will add T2 with a different mechanism: price sensitivity and retail availability as the binding cause of household vacuum purchases, which predicts no premium advantage. This gives T1 and T2 different, measurable predictions to assess and test.

examples.question: It is mid-1991. Should Diatek Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its infrared ear thermometer for hospitals? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources_read.diatek-spinoff-device: 1991 (originally published; note on later acquisition added afterwards)

arguments.claim: Parents of young children treat fever as a stressful event and dislike inserting or holding a thermometer in a sick child. If a fast, non-invasive ear thermometer were marketed for home pediatric use, parents would switch from glass or standard electronic thermometers and pay a premium, letting Diatek capture value via a differentiated pediatric home product.
arguments.who_benefits: Parents and caregivers of infants and young children, especially during nighttime fever episodes.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Existing home thermometers are slow, require contact or insertion, and upset sick children; a two-second eardrum reading removes that friction and anxiety.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Premium-priced consumer device positioned for pediatric home use, sold through pharmacies or direct mail, with the hospital brand lending credibility.
assumptions: Infrared ear readings are accurate and safe enough for home use and are cleared for consumer sale.
Parents will pay a meaningful premium over cheap digital/oral thermometers.
predictions: In a concept test, parents of children under 5 would choose the ear thermometer over a standard digital thermometer even at 3-5x the price.
Stated purchase intent is highest for the 'sick child at night' use case.

justification.learned: Sources diatek-jpl-market and diatek-spinoff-device show Diatek's Model 7000 aural/infrared ear thermometer reached the market in 1991, weighing eight ounces and reading in under two seconds, aimed at hospitals/doctors' offices; diatek-jpl-tap shows JPL TAP assistance. None of the three read sources says Diatek already sells to individual buyers, so consumer reach is unestablished. My repeated "Diatek consumer thermometer" searches were refused as duplicates. Unread results diatek-patent-rival and diatek-pm-zones remain.
justification.uncertain: Whether Diatek already reaches individual buyers, whether parents would pay a premium for home use, and the competitive/regulatory landscape. No consumer demand evidence has been read yet.
justification.why_next: The stage needs at least two causal theories and I have none. I add T1 now: a speed/comfort mechanism for pediatric home use, using the Model 7000's two-second non-invasive reading (diatek-spinoff-device) as the product fact while the hospital-only evidence (diatek-jpl-market) leaves consumer demand open. Next I will read diatek-patent-rival and diatek-pm-zones before adding T2 and T3.
