examples.question: It is late 2014. Should Perrigo develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its over-the-counter medicine development and manufacturing? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: European OTC buyers choose recognised symptom-specific brands (e.g. Solpadeine for pain, Nytol for sleep) over commodity generics because brand trust and pharmacy habit reduce perceived risk; a manufacturer that owns both the branded formulation and low-cost production can differentiate for that use case and capture the brand premium.
arguments.who_benefits: Consumers treating specific acute symptoms (pain, heartburn, sleeplessness) who already buy branded OTC rather than store brands.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: They reuse brands they trust and that pharmacists stock; owning the brand lets Perrigo position the product for the exact use case instead of competing only as a low-price store-brand supplier.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Premium retail pricing and repeat purchases of owned branded OTC, plus retained manufacturing margin, instead of only B2B store-brand supply fees.
assumptions: Omega's acquired brands retain consumer trust, pharmacy placement and rights after the 2014 deal.
Brand trust extends to new variants aimed at the same specific use case.
Perrigo can market owned brands without losing store-brand supply contracts.
predictions: Markets where Perrigo owns a specific-use brand show higher unit share and price premium than comparable store-brand or generic equivalents.
Consumers show higher repeat purchase for the owned brand in its use case than for a generic alternative.
Pharmacies continue stocking the acquired brand after the deal.

justification.learned: Perrigo already reaches individual buyers indirectly through store brands: its Barclays presentation says store-brand Cetirizine reached 48% penetration (perrigo-bar-penetration). FundingUniverse notes that deep price gaps once made consumers suspicious of the Perrigo brand and drove them to national brands (perrigo-fu-suspicious). The November 2014 Omega deal gives Perrigo owned branded OTC products for specific use cases—Solpadeine, Zantac, Nytol, Beconase, Lactacyd, Abtei (perrigo-pml-gsk)—and makes it the fifth-largest European OTC player (perrigo-ppr-omega). No causal theory has been added yet; the stage requires at least two.
justification.uncertain: No source read so far shows consumer demand for a new Perrigo-branded differentiated proposition, only the existence of acquired brands and store-brand penetration. It is unknown whether the acquired brands retain consumer trust and pharmacy placement, whether a consumer proposition would cannibalise or anger retail B2B partners, and financial returns are not in the dossier.

examples.question: It is mid-2013. Should FLIR Systems develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its uncooled thermal imaging cores? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Consumers who need to see heat for a concrete job (hunters locating game, homeowners finding heat leaks or electrical faults) currently go without because professional imagers cost thousands. Once a purpose-built device fits that job at a sub-$1,000 price, these buyers switch from guessing or binoculars to buying it, and FLIR captures value through premium-priced hardware over its uncooled core.
arguments.who_benefits: Hunters, outdoor recreation users and DIY homeowners/small-property owners who need to see heat to find animals, leaks or faults.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: A task-specific device below the professional price threshold removes cost and complexity barriers, so these buyers purchase a dedicated tool instead of doing without.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: FLIR sells the device at consumer prices well above core cost and earns follow-on sales of accessories, apps or upgrades tied to the use case.
assumptions: The use case is frequent and valuable enough to justify a $500-$1,000 purchase.
Target buyers can interpret thermal images without expert training.
FLIR can reach consumers through retail or direct channels.
Uncooled core cost leaves room for consumer margins.
predictions: Hunters and DIYers shown a sub-$1,000 purpose-built camera state higher purchase intent than for a generic professional model.
In a deposit test, sign-up rate in the target segment exceeds 5% of viewers.

examples.question: Should ARRI develop a differentiated proposition of its own for individual creators, beyond its professional cinema range and its smartphone partnership, or keep its consumer presence to partners? What evidence would justify either choice?

arguments.claim: Individual creators covet ARRI's cinematic look and brand prestige but can only use ARRI gear via rentals or partners, so an affordable ARRI-branded creator product sold directly would make them buy to own the ARRI identity instead of borrowing it.
arguments.who_benefits: Individual video creators (indie filmmakers, YouTubers, solo content creators) who cannot justify ARRI's $55,000 cinema cameras.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: ARRI is 'a brand they use rather than a brand they own' (arri-ymc-use-not-own); the HONOR deal offers 'more creators access to greater creative control' (arri-honor-milestone), making ARRI ownership attainable.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ARRI sells affordable hardware or licensed look/software directly at a premium over commodity creator gear, capturing margin beyond rental and studio sales.
assumptions: Creators value the ARRI brand enough to pay more than alternatives
ARRI can launch an affordable product without cannibalising professional sales
Aspiration converts into actual purchases, not just admiration
predictions: Creators who now only rent or use ARRI via partners show higher purchase intent for an affordable ARRI product than for rivals
An ARRI-branded creator product commands a price premium over an unbranded equivalent
Direct sales to individuals grow without reducing professional rental revenue

examples.question: It is late 2002. Should KES Science & Technology develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its photocatalytic air purifier for food storage and commercial buildings? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: In late 2002, post-anthrax bioterrorism anxiety made consumers value actively pathogen-destroying air purification in private spaces, so a device positioned on killing airborne pathogens (not on ethylene/gas removal) would drive premium household and small-office purchases.
arguments.who_benefits: Homeowners and small clinics/offices worried about airborne pathogens after the 2001 anthrax attacks.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Fear of anthrax and infectious airborne disease shifts buying from ordinary air cleaning toward devices that demonstrably kill pathogens as air passes through.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: KES sells a differentiated, premium-priced consumer unit built on the NASA-validated TiO2 pathogen-killing claim, capturing margin directly rather than licensing.
assumptions: A consumer unit can be made safe, quiet and affordable for homes by late 2002
The 93.3% pathogen-kill claim is credible, permitted and transferable to a home device
A retail or direct channel can reach these buyers profitably
predictions: Consumers shown a pathogen-killing claim will show higher stated purchase intent or purchase rate than those shown a general air-cleaning claim
Private-space buyers in testimonials will cite pathogen/health protection rather than food freshness as their reason

examples.question: Should Cotral Lab develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing hearing-protection offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Professional musicians will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a performanceenhancing tool that preserves sound quality while blocking noise, because they value accurate sound and are willing to pay a premium for a product that does not compromise their craft.
theories.T2: Sleep aid users will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a medical-grade solution that reduces sleep disruption caused by background noise, because they seek a product that addresses a specific health concern and are willing to pay for a solution that improves sleep quality.

justification.learned: Cotral Lab makes custom-moulded hearing protection, acquired by Groupe RG, and sells "primarily through direct channels to end-user companies" (ctl-channel, ctl-deal), so consumer reach is likely limited. Capability claims cover 3D printing (ctl-3d), in-house filters (ctl-filter), on-site impressions (ctl-onsite) and Bluetooth plugs (ctl-it1). bockstael-2015-looks: musicians' appreciation "mainly depended on comfort and looks", not sound quality. minuendo-claim shows a rival musician earplug exists. Theories T1 (musicians) and T2 (sleep aid) are on file but demand is unproven; the T1 revision wrongly leaned on simulated SYN-C, so finish was refused.
justification.uncertain: Whether professional musicians or sleep-aid users would actually purchase and pay a premium for a Cotral Lab consumer proposition is unknown. bockstael-2015-looks is appreciation, not purchasing behaviour, and minuendo-claim is a competitor's capability claim, not demand. T2 has no demand-bearing evidence at all. One real source, etymotic-er20xs, is still unread and may bear on musician earplugs and the T1 mechanism.
justification.why_next: The last calls were refused because SYN-C (simulated) was cited to support a real-demand recommendation. Before any finish or revise_theory, I should read the one unread source etymotic-er20xs, which is real evidence on musician earplugs, so I can assess it against T1 and remove the simulated result from any final recommendation.

arguments.target_customer: Professional musicians (live performers, studio musicians) who need hearing protection for performances and studio work.
arguments.value_proposition: Custom-moulded hearing protection marketed as a performanceenhancing tool that preserves sound quality, leveraging Cotral Lab’s 3D printing precision and comfort to justify a premium price.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed musician vs sleep aid purchase intent survey (400 respondents, 6 weeks, €15,000) to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay for the performanceenhancing version.

examples.question: It is late 2017. Should Lenzing AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its lyocell and modal fibres? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Shoppers who already weigh fibre origin (e.g., organic-cotton percentage) would switch to or pay more for garments whose lyocell/modal origin is made legible through a trusted consumer brand, because clear ingredient marking resolves uncertainty about man-made cellulosic fibres.
arguments.who_benefits: Sustainability-motivated apparel shoppers and the brands/retailers that serve them.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: These shoppers already use fibre content as a deciding attribute; a recognisable TENCEL/Refibra mark turns an invisible B2B ingredient into a visible, trusted cue, raising purchase likelihood and willingness to pay.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Lenzing earns ingredient-brand pull-through and premium fibre pricing; brands pay to use a differentiated certified fibre that wins these shoppers.
assumptions: A segment weighs fibre origin for MMCFs, not just cotton
Brands pass the ingredient story through to hangtags
Lenzing can protect and enforce the consumer brand
The uplift exceeds marketing cost
predictions: Shoppers shown a TENCEL/Refibra hangtag on identical garments choose them more often and state higher willingness to pay than those shown an unbranded lyocell tag
Brands carrying the certified fibre report higher sell-through in eco-conscious channels

justification.learned: Read so far: lyocell demand grew 128% in 2017 (lenzing-te2017-lyocell); Zara/Inditex sells Refibra clothing as first strategic partner (lenzing-ar16-zara, company claim); Lenzing has owned Tencel since 2000 (lenzing-wiki-tencel1992); 2006 study: 53% of two segments used organic-cotton % to decide purchase likelihood (lenzing-hustvedt-organic); 2024 survey (post-dates decision) says only 13% felt MMCF label info sufficient (lenzing-pefc-labels). justification.uncertain: Whether 2006 organic-cotton attribute use transfers to man-made cellulosic fibres in late 2017; whether Lenzing already reaches individual buyers (unread lenzing-pr18-b2b2c, lenzing-pr18-research, lenzing-wtin-swingtags); whether a consumer proposition lets Lenzing capture premium value or brands capture it.

examples.question: It is 1924. Should Leitz develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its precision optics and a small-format camera that its development head built to test cinema film exposures? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: In 1924 amateur and outdoor photographers are constrained by bulky, slow large-format equipment; a pocketable 35mm camera using cheap cinema film lets them carry a camera more often and take many candid exposures, so they would adopt it even though some Leitz managers doubt series production.
arguments.who_benefits: Amateur hobbyists and outdoor/sports photographers who want portability and spontaneous candid shots.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Lower bulk and lower per-exposure film cost reduce the effort and expense per photograph, shifting behaviour from occasional formal plate photography to frequent spontaneous photography.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Leitz sells the camera as a premium precision instrument and captures further value from lenses, enlargers and accessories; buyers' repeat film use sustains demand for Leitz enlarging equipment.
assumptions: 35mm negatives can be enlarged to acceptable print quality for hobbyists.
Hobbyists value portability and candid capability over large-format detail.
Leitz can reach individual buyers through retailers or direct sales.
The camera is reliable enough for everyday use.
predictions: When offered both a plate camera and the 35mm compact, outdoor/amateur photographers choose the 35mm for field and candid use.
Pre-production outdoor photographers express willingness to buy or order the camera.
Individual-buyer sales of the camera and accessories rise once it is offered to consumers.

examples.question: It is 1928. Should Carrier Engineering Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its refrigeration and humidity-control engineering? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Affluent homeowners in hot, humid cities see indoor comfort as a luxury they cannot yet obtain at home; if Carrier offers engineered residential 'manufactured weather' as a prestige comfort system, these households would buy it despite high cost.

arguments.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from tolerating heat or using fans/ice to buying an installed system because home comfort and modern prestige become attainable and worth the price.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Carrier captures value through premium engineering, installation and service contracts on each home system.

predictions: High-income urban households will make inquiries or deposits for home systems

Buyers pay a premium over simple fans or window units

examples.question: It is late 1974. Should Statitrol Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its ionization smoke-detection technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Homeowners only act on fire risk when protection is a cheap, self-installable product rather than an electrical project; the 1974 NFPA 74 change legitimising battery-operated units removes that friction, so a maker selling a simple battery ionization detector through mass retail can capture volume.
arguments.who_benefits: Homeowners and renters in older homes who cannot afford or retrofit hard-wired AC smoke detectors.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Hard-wired detectors require mains power and electrician installation, which is costly and slow; a battery unit is a low-cost, minutes-long purchase, so people who previously never acted on fire risk start buying.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Statitrol earns margin on high-volume battery units sold through retail channels instead of low-volume installed industrial systems.

Mass retailers will stock and promote a Statitrol or Statitrol-made unit
Homeowners perceive fire risk as worth a modest one-time purchase
predictions: In a retail trial, low-priced battery units sell in meaningful volume with no installer involvement
Households without hard-wired systems buy at higher rates than households with them
Sales rise after the 1974 NFPA 74 change rather than before it

arguments.claim: People who must wear safety or work footwear for long hours suffer chronic foot pain and treat comfort as the scarce attribute. arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Comfort and quality, not just certification or price, are their top purchase priorities; they currently accept pain as unavoidable, so a proven pain-relieving option makes them switch and pay a premium.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Sievi charges premium prices for comfort-differentiated, certified models and earns repeat purchases and loyalty through retailers such as Karkkainen or direct channels.

Sievi can credibly differentiate on measurable comfort while keeping safety certification.
predictions: Workers buying their own shoes choose comfort-led models over cheaper certified alternatives.
Stated and actual willingness to pay a premium is higher for comfort claims than for generic safety shoes.

Leitz can build the camera reliably at a cost below what amateurs will pay.
A route to individual buyers exists or can be built at acceptable cost.
predictions: In a 1924 trial, outdoor photographers given the compact camera would take more exposures per outing than with a plate camera.

examples.question: Should Festool develop a differentiated proposition for hobbyist woodworkers, beyond its existing offering, or keep a single range for all buyers? What evidence would justify either choice?

arguments.claim: Hobbyist woodworkers buy Festool primarily as an aspirational signal of owning professional-grade tools. The brand's value to them is that it is the same expensive range professionals use, so a visibly cheaper 'hobbyist' line would weaken the status signal and reduce, not expand, hobbyist demand.
arguments.who_benefits: Hobbyists who use the brand to signal seriousness, skill, and professional-grade standards to themselves and peers.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: A cheaper hobbyist range would mean owning real Festool no longer marks a serious, professional-grade woodworker, so hobbyists would buy less of the premium line or switch brands.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Festool keeps one premium-priced range and captures high margin per unit from hobbyists who pay up for the professional halo; differentiation would cannibalise that margin without adding enough new buyers.
assumptions: Hobbyist buyers are motivated more by aspiration/status than by pure price.
The professional halo is what makes the premium price acceptable to hobbyists.
A cheaper line would be visibly distinguishable and would dilute the brand's exclusivity.
predictions: A majority of hobbyists would continue to buy the existing premium range even when a cheaper Festool line is available.
A differentiated lower-priced hobbyist line would attract few new buyers and would lower average margin per unit.
Hobbyists who already own Festool would not trade down to a cheaper line in significant numbers.

justification.learned: I have read four sources. festool-fww-price shows hobbyists' dominant reaction is premium-price perception ('Why are they so expensive?'). festool-mix and festool-hobby-growth (Core77, 2015) show the buyer mix shifted from ~70/30 hobbyist/professional in 2004-05 to ~60/40 professional/hobbyist, and that the professional segment is growing faster. festool-woodcraft-origin shows early hobbyist draw came through a dealer (Woodcraft) that catered to hobbyists with limited distribution. No theories have been added yet, and the stage requires at least two with different causes.
justification.uncertain: The mechanism behind hobbyist purchasing is unresolved: whether hobbyists buy Festool for professional-grade status/aspiration (and would reject a cheaper 'hobbyist' line) or are price-constrained (and would respond to a cheaper, simplified range). Demand is not established. Unread sources festool-bigbox and festool-ukw-overpaid have not been read and may bear on distribution and hobbyist pricing feelings.
justification.why_next: The stage needs theories (0 of 2). I am adding T1 first, a status/aspiration mechanism drawn from festool-fww-price (premium price perception) and festool-mix (professional halo as the mix shifted pro-ward). I will then read festool-bigbox and festool-ukw-overpaid and add a rival price-constraint theory (T2) so the two mechanisms can be tested against each other.

examples.question: It is mid-1981. Should G.D. Searle develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its aspartame sweetener? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Consumers avoid sugar for weight and health reasons but are put off by saccharin's bitter aftertaste; because aspartame removes that aftertaste while eliminating 95.5% of sugar's calories, individual buyers would switch to aspartame-sweetened products for specific uses (diet beverages, tabletop sweetener) and pay a premium.
arguments.who_benefits: Diet- and health-conscious individual buyers (weight watchers, diabetics) and any seller that controls an aspartame-based consumer brand.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: The previous barrier to switching — saccharin's bitter aftertaste — disappears while the calorie/health motive remains, so the taste-versus-calorie trade-off no longer suppresses purchase.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Searle builds a differentiated consumer proposition (e.g., a branded tabletop sweetener or diet product) and earns premium retail margins rather than commodity ingredient margins.
assumptions: Taste is a real barrier to saccharin adoption among consumers
Searle can reach individual buyers directly or through a branded retail product
The July 1981 FDA approval opens a consumer tabletop and food-additive market
Consumers will pay a premium for better taste at near-zero calories
predictions: In a blind taste test, diet-conscious consumers rate an aspartame-sweetened product higher than a saccharin one and choose it at a higher rate
A branded aspartame product for a specific use captures measurable trial and repeat purchases at a price premium over saccharin

justification.learned: Read sources establish product facts and regulatory status, not demand. searle-sfu-aftertaste: aspartame "lacked the bitter aftertaste of saccharin and eliminated 95.5 percent of the calories of sugar." searle-sfu-july1981: July 1981 FDA approval opened tabletop sweetener and food-additive use. searle-csm-neversees (1984): "The consumer never sees NutraSweet, but tastes it in a variety of soft drinks" — consumers meet it through manufacturers. searle-sfu-dramamine shows Searle has some retail reach in medicines. No source yet shows individual demand or willingness to pay; unread results searle-csm-research and searle-nfu-patent remain.
justification.uncertain: Whether individual buyers would actually switch or pay a premium for an aspartame-sweetened product; Searle's existing retail/distribution reach beyond medicines; whether manufacturers, not consumers, are the true purchasers. arguments.why_behaviour_changes: They frame home fitness as décor and status, so buying is driven by aesthetics and brand, not by gym access, necessity or lowest price.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Technogym earns premium margins and repeat purchases across a design-led home collection plus paid interior-design guidance.

examples.question: Should Hilti develop a differentiated proposition for home users or hobbyists, beyond its existing professional offering, or leave that market alone? What evidence would justify either choice?

arguments.claim: Hilti's professional customers pay premium prices partly because the brand signals uncompromising, professional-only quality and a restricted B2B channel reinforces that. A separate lower-cost home-user line would blur this exclusivity signal, making pros compare Hilti to DIY brands and lowering their willingness to pay the premium, so lost pro margin could exceed any consumer volume gained.
arguments.who_benefits: Construction professionals and contractors who use Hilti as a credible signal of industrial-grade, professional-only quality.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Pros currently accept premium prices because Hilti is seen as professional-only; a visible consumer line would weaken that signal and push them toward cheaper pro/DIY alternatives.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Hilti captures value through premium pricing and repeat purchases by professionals; dilution of the exclusivity signal would erode margin on the larger, higher-margin pro base.
assumptions: Professionals treat brand exclusivity as a buying signal, not only tool performance
Hilti's premium rests partly on reputation rather than durability alone
A consumer line would be visible to and noticed by professional buyers
predictions: If Hilti launches a consumer line, professional customers' stated willingness to pay premium falls versus a control
Pro share or repeat purchase of Hilti declines after a consumer launch while DIY demand stays price-sensitive
Retail/direct availability of consumer Hilti correlates with pro customers discounting the brand

justification.learned: From hilti-b2b-reach, Hilti is primarily B2B and "hasn't done much to reach individual end users", though Home Depot now sells Hilti Nuron tools. From hilti-consumers-price-sensitive, consumers "are very price sensitive... opting for less costly imports over expensive professional-grade models." No source yet shows actual home-user demand for Hilti or whether a consumer move would dilute the pro brand; several unread sources (hilti-direct-model, hilti-hd-exit, hilti-downscale-dilution, hilti-hd-rental, hilti-craftsman-pro-label) may bear on this.
justification.uncertain: Whether Hilti's existing route to individual buyers is retail, direct e-commerce, or rental (hilti-direct-model, hilti-hd-exit, hilti-hd-rental unread); whether a downscale consumer line would actually dilute Hilti's professional signal (hilti-downscale-dilution unread); and whether any home users would actually buy Hilti at premium prices.

examples.question: It is late 1978. Should Texas Instruments develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its microprocessor and chip technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated TI microprocessor-based consumer product if it offers a clear, fun educational experience that demonstrates the technology's capabilities.

arguments.claim: Consumers treat electronics as ordinary consumer goods bought on price, styling and everyday usefulness, not on underlying chip technology, so a differentiated TI device will win individual buyers only if it is styled and priced like competing consumer products, an area where TI's own watch business already failed.
arguments.who_benefits: Price-sensitive mass-market shoppers wanting everyday utility; TI would profit through high volume at category prices, not novelty premiums.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: TI's LCD watches lost to styling issues, excessive model variety and price points, showing buyers reward appearance and price over chip novelty.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: TI sells through mass retailers at or below established consumer-electronics prices, earning margin from its chip cost advantage and scale rather than from differentiation.
assumptions: 1978 consumer-electronics purchases are driven mainly by price and style, not component technology.
TI can match consumer brands on styling and retail price.
TI's chip cost advantage lowers its end-product cost enough to sustain low prices.
predictions: A premium-priced novelty TI device will undersell comparable lower-priced consumer products.
A low-priced, well-styled TI version will outsell a premium novelty version of the same device.
TI consumer products priced above category norms will repeat the LCD-watch failure pattern.

examples.question: It is mid-1991. Should Diatek Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its infrared ear thermometer for hospitals? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Parents will adopt a consumer infrared ear thermometer if it is marketed as a quick, accurate, and safe alternative to mercury thermometers, because they currently struggle to read traditional thermometers.
theories.T2: Parents will adopt a consumer infrared ear thermometer if it is marketed as a convenient, non‑contact alternative to mercury thermometers, because they currently struggle to read traditional thermometers and prefer quick measurements.

sources_read.diatek-spinoff-device: 1991 (originally published; note on later acquisition added afterwards)

arguments.reason: SYN-D is a simulated warehouse test about a label printer reducing packing errors; it measured nothing about wearers or buyers, so it bears on neither T1 nor T2 and cannot change confidence in either. T2 is likewise unchanged. No revision is warranted.

justification.learned: SYN-D is a simulated warehouse test showing a new label printer reduced packing errors slightly; it measured nothing about wearers or buyers. It bears on neither T1 nor T2: both concern parents adopting an infrared ear thermometer versus mercury thermometers, and packing-error data cannot speak to parent purchase behaviour or the accuracy/safety (T1) versus convenience/speed (T2) motives. So it changes nothing. Remaining market evidence: diatek-pm-zones (reading difficulty, independent study), diatek-jpl-market and diatek-spinoff-device (product existence/capability, not demand), diatek-patent-rival (competitor aim). None shows actual switching or willingness to pay.
justification.uncertain: Consumer demand remains unknown: nothing read shows parents would actually switch to, or pay a premium for, an infrared ear thermometer. Willingness to pay, the specific use case, competitive positioning versus Thermoscan (diatek-patent-rival), and regulatory feasibility for a consumer device are all unmeasured. T1 (accuracy/safety driver) is favoured only weakly, and T2 (convenience/speed driver) is uncertain; the proposed test X1 is still the main way to separate them.
justification.why_next: Because SYN-D is irrelevant, keep T1 and T2 as open and retain the existing position. The next action is to run the Consumer Preference Test (X1), which measures purchase intent and primary reasons among parents and is the only proposed discriminator between T1 (accuracy/safety cited) and T2 (convenience/speed cited) against a digital thermometer baseline. It relies on diatek-pm-zones for the reading-difficulty premise, and its decision rule (infrared purchase intent at least 20 percentage points above digital, with the distinguishing reason cited) is unchanged.

examples.question: It is early 2011. Should MSA (Mine Safety Appliances) develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its respirators, hard hats and fall-protection products? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Homeowners under 35 will purchase MSA consumer safety products primarily for DIY projects because they view safety gear as essential for completing tasks safely.
theories.T2: Homeowners under 35 will purchase MSA consumer safety products primarily for outdoor recreation activities because they view safety gear as essential for protecting themselves and their gear in nature-based settings.

arguments.reason: The simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) measured a label printer's effect on packing errors, not consumer behaviour, so it cannot support, contradict, or revise T1's claim that under-35 homeowners buy safety gear as essential for DIY.

justification.learned: The simulated result (SYN-D) shows only that a warehouse label printer reduced packing errors slightly; it measured nothing about wearers, buyers, or consumer demand. It bears on neither T1 nor T2, because both theories explain why homeowners under 35 would buy consumer safety gear (DIY vs outdoor recreation), and an internal warehouse/logistics outcome cannot confirm or disconfirm either mechanism. I therefore keep T1 and T2 unchanged and open. The evidence that still matters is the independent DIY-spending share among under-35 owners (msa-jchs-diy) and MSA's existing retail reach (msa-jv-1998, msa-jv-retailers, msa-jv-storefronts).
justification.uncertain: Consumer demand remains unproven. The dossier shows MSA entered consumer retail in 1998 (msa-jv-1998) and reaches 10,000+ storefronts (msa-jv-storefronts), and that under-35 owners devoted 29% of improvement spending to DIY in 2011 (msa-jchs-diy). examples.question: It is mid-2025. Should Netafim develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its drip-irrigation technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt Netafim's drip irrigation kits because they perceive them as a healthful, eco-friendly alternative to sprinkler systems, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt Netafim's drip irrigation kits because they perceive them as a convenient, low‑maintenance solution for small urban gardens and balconies, leading to higher purchase frequency and repeat purchases.

arguments.reason: The simulated result SYN-D measures only a label printer's effect on warehouse packing errors; it does not measure consumers, buyers, irrigation kit adoption, or Netafim demand, so it neither supports nor contradicts T1 (or T2) and cannot move confidence.

justification.learned: SYN-D (simulated warehouse test) concerns a label printer reducing packing errors; it measured nothing about consumers, buyers, irrigation kits, or Netafim, so it bears on neither T1 (eco-conscious adoption) nor T2 (convenience adoption) and changes no belief. Real evidence on record: CSU's independent figure (drip exceeds 90% efficiency vs 50-70% for sprinklers) supports T1's water-saving mechanism but not willingness to pay; Netafim's own home-kit pages (netafim-in-homekit, netafim-in-nonexpert, netafim-in-variants) show products exist and target small spaces — capability/feasibility, not proof of consumer motivation. Public demand or sales data for a consumer proposition remain absent.
justification.uncertain: Whether any consumer segment would actually pay a premium for an eco or convenience positioning is still unknown. No source found shows demand, sales, or willingness to pay; company assertions establish feasibility, not purchasing behaviour. T1 has an independent efficiency fact in its favour but no evidence consumers pay more for it; T2 rests only on Netafim's own product descriptions. Both theories are under-evidenced on the demand and value-capture links.
justification.why_next: Because SYN-D is irrelevant to both theories, beliefs should not move: T1 stays likely, T2 stays uncertain, and overall confidence remains low. The next discriminating action is the proposed choice experiment X1, which measures consequential choice and willingness-to-pay and separates T1's eco premium prediction from T2's convenience premium prediction under a stated threshold; a later pilot measuring actual purchases would be needed because X1 captures stated intent, not sales.

examples.question: It is mid-2013. Should FLIR Systems develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its uncooled thermal imaging cores? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T2: Consumers will adopt thermal imaging devices if they experience the technology firsthand through a demo or trial, because they need to validate performance before committing to a purchase.

arguments.reason: SYN-D is a simulated warehouse test showing a label printer reduced packing errors slightly and measured nothing about wearers or buyers. arguments.reason: SYN-D is a simulated warehouse test measuring label-printer packing errors only. justification.learned: The simulated result (SYN-D) measured only warehouse operations—a new label printer that "reduced packing errors slightly." It therefore bears on neither T1 (low-price medical adoption) nor T2 (fashion/status adoption), because both theories make claims about why parents would purchase an infant warmer, and this result contains no observation about that behaviour. I record T1 as kept and, by the same logic, T2 also remains unchanged: the result changes nothing about what we believe regarding demand.
justification.uncertain: The core uncertainty is unchanged: none of the public sources show actual parent purchase behaviour or demand for a consumer infant warmer, only product origin, price listings, a company SIDS claim, and launch/use in India. The simulated warehouse result cannot fill that gap, so belief in T1 remains "likely" and T2 "uncertain" on the strength of the existing (weak, largely company-sourced) evidence, not on SYN-D.
justification.why_next: Because SYN-D is irrelevant to both T1 and T2, no theory revision is warranted beyond recording it as a no-change result. If X1 shows T1's condition reaches the 30% purchase-intent threshold with safety/SIDS cited by at least 60%, proceed toward a medical consumer proposition; otherwise keep focus on the existing B2B route (or no expansion).

examples.question: Should Koppert develop a differentiated proposition for home gardeners, building on its biological crop protection for professional growers, or stay with professional growers? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Home gardeners will adopt Koppert's biological controls if they perceive them as convenient, easy to use, and safe for children and pets, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay a premium.
theories.T2: Home gardeners will adopt Koppert's biological controls if they perceive them as a status symbol or a way to differentiate their garden, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay a premium.

arguments.name: Home-gardener paid pre-order positioning test
arguments.method: Target customers: Dutch home gardeners who bought a garden pest-control product in the last 12 months, recruited online. Treatment: Two arms, same lady beetles and price: (A) a ready-to-use release tube with 'safe for children and pets, open and release' messaging (T1 mechanism); (B) a premium presentation box with 'a garden to be proud of' messaging (T2 mechanism). Control: A plain professional-style sachet with technical instructions only; same lady beetles and same price.
arguments.sample: 900 home gardeners (300 per arm) in the Netherlands, recruited via Dutch gardening Facebook groups and garden-center email newsletters, screened for a garden pest-control purchase in the past 12 months, then randomly assigned.
arguments.measure: Paid pre-order conversion: share of visitors in each arm who complete a €5 deposit toward a spring shipment of a lady-beetle release pack, tracked by unique link.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A (safety/ease) has the highest paid pre-order rate, at least 8 percentage points above control and at least 5 points above arm B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B (premium/status) has the highest paid pre-order rate, at least 8 percentage points above control and at least 5 points above arm A.

arguments.decision_rule: Develop the home proposition only if one arm's paid pre-order rate beats control by at least 8 percentage points AND beats the other arm by at least 5 points; the winning arm sets the positioning. If neither arm beats control by at least 8 points, stay with professional growers. If arm A wins: run a garden-center pilot of a ready-to-use safety/ease line. If arm B wins: run a specialty-retail pilot of a premium presentation line. If neither beats control: stay focused on professional growers and do not build a home line.

justification.learned: Koppert already reaches individual buyers: koppert-lo-canada says Koppert Canada serves "the professional grower and the home gardening enthusiast"; koppert-martha-visit shows a garden visit; koppert-wsu-shipped says lady beetles are "shipped to farmers and home gardeners alike". koppert-about-founded is only a founding story. koppert-agro-ban shows France banning non-agricultural pesticide sales from Jan 2019 (opportunity but regulatory risk). None quantify home-gardener demand, willingness to pay, or adoption; demand is unknown. The "supports" ratings for T1/T2 reflect existence/capability, not proven demand.
justification.uncertain: Whether measurable home-gardener demand exists; no source shows purchases, repeat use, or willingness to pay. Which mechanism drives buying: T1 (safety/convenience) or T2 (status/premium). Whether biological controls for amateurs are legally sellable in the EU after France's 2019 non-agricultural pesticide ban, and whether live-organism products can be profitably shipped to consumers. Sources predate 2026, so current demand is unverified.
justification.why_next: The decision depends on observable demand, which the dossier does not establish. A paid pre-order test separates T1 from T2 because each predicts its own positioning variant wins on real deposits, and it separates expansion from staying if neither variant beats the neutral control. I rely on T1 and T2 and on koppert-lo-canada (capability to reach enthusiasts) and koppert-agro-ban (regulatory context).

examples.question: It is mid-2013. Should FLIR Systems develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its uncooled thermal imaging cores? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt thermal imaging devices if they perceive them as a safety or utility product for home use, because they value the ability to detect heat signatures for fire detection, home maintenance, or outdoor activities.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt thermal imaging devices if they perceive them as a utility product for outdoor recreation and hunting, because they value the ability to detect heat signatures for tracking game, navigation, or safety.

arguments.name: Paid reservation A/B test: home-safety vs outdoor thermal camera bundles
arguments.method: Target customers: US adults aged 25-60 who own a home and also hunt or do outdoor recreation at least monthly, screened via a targeted online panel. Treatment: A landing page for 'FLIR Home Monitor' at $499: an uncooled-core thermal camera that attaches to a phone, plus a wall mount, continuous power, a high-temperature audible alarm, and an energy/water-leak audit guide, positioned as a home-safety/utility tool. Page template, price and deposit ask are identical to the control. Control: A landing page for 'FLIR Field Scout' at $499: the same uncooled-core thermal camera that attaches to a phone, plus weatherproof housing, 8-hour battery, handheld grip, rail mount and lanyard, positioned for spotting game and night navigation. Page template, price and deposit ask are identical to the treatment.
arguments.sample: Recruit 800 participants (400 per arm) over three weeks from a US online panel, screened for home ownership and monthly hunting/outdoor recreation, then randomized to one landing page.
arguments.measure: Share of participants who complete a $20 refundable deposit to reserve the $499 product within 14 days of seeing the page; deposits are refunded after the test.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The home-safety bundle has a deposit rate at least 3 percentage points higher than the outdoor bundle.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The outdoor bundle has a deposit rate at least 3 percentage points higher than the home-safety bundle.

arguments.decision_rule: The winning bundle must reach at least a 5% deposit rate, and beat the rival by at least 3 percentage points, to justify further investment. Below 5% or a margin under 3 points means no consumer launch now. If home-safety wins (at least 5% deposit rate and at least 3 points ahead), run a bounded 500-unit pilot with one home-improvement retail partner. If outdoor wins on the same criteria, run a bounded 500-unit pilot with one outdoor specialty retailer. If neither reaches 5% or the margin is under 3 points, do not expand to consumers now; continue the B2B/no-expansion route and re-test only if core cost falls or a partner shows demand evidence.

justification.learned: Pre-mid-2013 sources show FLIR had a low-cost prosumer camera, not a consumer line: the i3 launched Feb 2011 at US$1,195, "the most affordable high-quality infrared camera" for "every electrician and engineer" (flir-eb-i3price; flir-mb-toolbox). Prices had "decreased continuously" (flir-mb-pricefall). A 2007 report shows thermal imaging sold as a $150+ technician service, not a consumer purchase (flir-spk-service). No pre-mid-2013 source shows individual buyers purchasing for home safety or hunting, or a retail/DTC channel; demand and willingness to pay are unknown. 2014 sources excluded.
justification.uncertain: The open question is whether any consumer use case would produce enough real commitment to justify a consumer line, and which motivation is stronger: home safety/utility (T1) or outdoor/hunting (T2). No pre-2013 source shows consumer price elasticity at a $499-$1,195 price, repeat purchase, channel economics, or purchase frequency. Low core cost alone does not establish consumer pull.
justification.why_next: This paid-reservation test is worth the proposed €18,000/8-week cost because it can change the decision: it measures deposits, not stated interest, and separates T1 from T2 because the home bundle embodies continuous home monitoring while the outdoor bundle embodies field use, so each theory predicts the opposite bundle wins among dual-motivated homeowners who also recreate outdoors. The 5% minimum-demand and 3-point margin thresholds stop the project if neither use case clears the bar. Limitation: bundle features could drive the margin rather than pure motivation, so the winning result only funds a 500-unit pilot, not a full product line.
